h1: Used Audi Q3: The Best & Worst Years to Buy (2026 Edition)

contentBlocks.text: Buying a used European luxury SUV always feels a bit risky. If you pick the right one, you get to drive a nice car without spending too much. But if you get the wrong one, you'll just end up paying your mechanic a lot of money.

The Audi Q3 has been a popular small luxury SUV in the US ever since it first came out for the 2015 model year. It uses the same basic parts as the VW Tiguan but looks more high-end with its Audi badge. Don't let the fancy looks fool you though—some years are reliable and great, while others are just terrible.
Before you buy one, here's a simple look at which Audi Q3 years are actually good buys and which ones will probably cost you a lot of money.
The Best Audi Q3 Years to Buy
If you want a luxury car without all the headaches, these are the only years you should even think about.
● 2017 Audi Q3: The Best Value
If you like how the first-generation Q3 looks but want to avoid the common early issues, the 2017 model is your best bet.

By this year, Audi had fixed the problems from earlier models. J.D. Power gave the car a good reliability score of 77 out of 100. Even better, the NHTSA only received four complaints for the whole year, which is really rare for a German luxury SUV.

Audi also made nice features like LED taillights and a panoramic sunroof standard on the basic model that year. It's not a race car, but the 200-horsepower turbo-four engine is smooth and reliable for city driving, and it won't suddenly leave you stranded.
● 2019 Audi Q3: New Look, More Technology

The 2019 model year brought in the second-generation platform, and Audi really changed things up. Edmunds' expert rating jumped from a mediocre 6.9 in 2018 to a strong 7.8 in 2019, and there was a good reason for that.

This year, they added the impressive Audi Virtual Cockpit, which replaced the old analog gauges with a sharp digital display. Usually, the first year of a brand-new design has a lot of electrical problems, but the 2019 Q3 was different. It had half as many complaints as the older model it replaced. If you're looking for modern tech without spending too much, this is a good place to start.
● 2021 & 2022 Audi Q3: Newer and Safer Options

If you can afford a newer car that's coming off a lease, these two years are the best of the second generation. The 2021 model improved a lot after the problematic 2020, getting a 77 out of 100 quality score from J.D. Power. The 2022 model kept up that good score with 78 out of 100. Audi really stepped up the tech features here, adding wireless Apple CarPlay, blind-spot monitoring, and rear cross-traffic alerts as standard. Buying one of these means you're getting a well-developed car with all the early software issues fixed.
Years to Avoid: The Audi Q3 Red Flags
Don't even think about these years. If a dealer tries to sell you one, just leave and don't look back.
● 2020 Audi Q3: A Complete Disaster
The 2020 model year was truly awful. It has the most NHTSA complaints of any Q3 year (over 40) and also a lot of recalls.

The big problem here is a serious sunroof drainage issue. When it rained, water often got past the cheap sunroof seals and dripped right into the overhead lights. This meant water could easily get into the car's main electrical system. Owners reported electrical shorts inside the car, fried USB ports, and worst of all, the whole car completely shutting down while driving on the highway. Audi's response to these upset owners wasn't very helpful. Just avoid this year completely.
● 2015 Audi Q3: The First Year, Not a Good One

Since this was the first year the Q3 came to the US, the 2015 model brought too many old European car problems with it. Yes, the MMI infotainment system feels super old, like it's from a 2004 flip phone, but that's the smallest issue.

The real big problem under the hood is a well-known issue with the timing chain tensioner. This car has an 'interference engine,' which means if that tensioner breaks and the chain slips even a little, the engine's internal parts will crash into each other violently. The engine basically blows up right away, and you'll be looking at a $6,000 to $8,000 bill to replace the whole thing.
● 2016 & 2018 Audi Q3: Not Great, Will Cost You Money

2016 Problems: This year had three different recalls for lighting issues, like turn signals and brake lights not working right. Plus, many people online have complained that the original windshields cracked for no clear reason.

2018 Problems: Experts only gave this year a 6.9 out of 10. It was the last year of the first-gen design, and it showed. The 6-speed automatic transmission was painfully slow and kept struggling to find the right gear. The gas mileage was also terrible for a small SUV. And for some reason, sunroofs would sometimes shatter suddenly, which was a scary problem that wasn't fixed.
What to Remember
Listen, no one cares about the Audi badge if your car is constantly on a tow truck. Don't buy a luxury car just to show off if it means you'll be at the repair shop all the time.

If you're looking for a used Q3, save your money by only considering a late first-generation model (2017) or a well-sorted, modern second-generation one (2019 or 2022). Make sure to get a clean Carfax report, check the front floor mats for any signs of sunroof leaks, and then you can actually enjoy the nice car you bought.
